name: Puppy & Pet Sale Scams
summary: Adverts for pedigree puppies at attractive prices collect deposits and escalating transport fees for an animal that does not exist.

typicalLoss.note: The emotional investment, often on behalf of children, keeps victims paying well past the point of doubt.

howItWorks.detail: Images are taken from legitimate breeders' websites or overseas social media. The same puppy appears in many adverts.
The seller is in another province, so viewing is impractical and transport is required. This is not incidental, it is the structure of the scam.
A deposit secures the puppy, usually by EFT, often with a plausible contract and vaccination records attached.
A crate deposit, a temperature-controlled carrier, pet insurance, a vet clearance certificate. Each is refundable on delivery. Each is paid because a family is now emotionally committed.

redFlags: Price well below what the breed normally sells for.
You cannot visit the animal or see its mother, in person or on a live video call.
Payment by EFT, e-wallet or crypto to an individual.
Escalating transport, crate, insurance or vet fees after the deposit.
The same photographs appear elsewhere online, or on other adverts.
illustrativeCase: A family pays a R4 500 deposit for a French bulldog puppy advertised from another province. A R3 200 climate-controlled crate deposit follows, then R2 800 for pet travel insurance, then R1 900 for a veterinary export certificate, each described as refundable on arrival. The delivery date passes three times before the number stops working.
howToProtect: Never buy an animal you or someone you trust has not physically seen, with its mother.
Insist on a live video call where you can ask the seller to do something specific with the puppy.
Reverse image search every photograph in the advert.
Buy through a KUSA-registered breeder, a recognised rescue organisation, or adopt from a shelter.
Treat any post-deposit fee as confirmation of fraud, not as an obstacle to overcome.
ifYouveBeenHit: Stop paying immediately, no matter how far in you are.
Report to your bank and request a recall.
Open a SAPS case and report the advert to the platform.
Warn breed groups and community pages, where these sellers recycle the same photographs.

faqs.q: They sent a video of the puppy.
faqs.a: Videos are stolen just as easily as photographs. Only a live call where the seller responds to your specific request proves anything.
Yes, with a legitimate breeder you have visited and verified. A deposit to a stranger you have not met, for an animal in another province, is the scam's basic shape.
